title: SemEval-2024, Task 8: Multigenerator, Multidomain, and Multilingual Black-Box Machine-Generated Text Detection
description: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming mainstream and easily accessible, ushering in an explosion of machine-generated content over various channels, such as news, social media, question-answering forums, educational, and even academic contexts. Recent LLMs, such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, generate remarkably fluent responses to a wide variety of user queries. The articulate nature of such generated texts makes LLMs attractive for replacing human labor in many scenarios. However, this has also resulted in concerns regarding their potential misuse, such as spreading misinformation and causing disruptions in the education system. Since humans perform only slightly better than chance when classifying machine-generated vs. human-written text, there is a need to develop automatic systems to identify machine-generated text with the goal of mitigating its potential misuse.\n\nWe offer three subtasks over two paradigms of text generation: (1) **full text** when a considered text is entirely written by a human or generated by a machine; and (2) **mixed text** when a machine-generated text is refined by a human or a human-written text paraphrased by a machine.

title: MICCAI 2024's DIAMOND
description:
Diabetic macular edema (DME) is a major complication of diabetes. Characterized by retinal thickening in the macula and often accompanied by hard exudate deposition, DME is a prevalent cause of vision loss among diabetic patients. The challenge's focus is on center-involved diabetic macular edema (ci-DME), a critical form of DME responsible for significant vision impairment. The presence of DME is generally assessed through 3D optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging. A recent study has shown that the presence of ci-DME can also be assessed using 2D color fundus photography (CFP). 

The DIAMOND challenge seeks to revolutionize the approach to diagnosing and treating ci-DME by integrating AI and deep learning with ultra-wide-field color fundus photography (UWF-CFP), a recent evolution of CFP. More challenging than assessing the presence of ci-DME, the goal is to develop and evaluate models that can predict if a patient will develop ci-DME within a year, using UWF-CFP images alone. Because it offers a much wider field of view, we hypothesize UWF-CFP is more likely to capture early signs of DME than standard CFP. Success in this challenge could significantly improve early detection and treatment planning, reduce vision loss incidents, and exemplify AI's efficacy in healthcare.

**Training Dataset and Initial Insights**
The challenge utilizes data sourced from 14 French hospitals as part of the EVIRED project (https://evired.org/). The project's broader goal is to predict ci-DME development and anticipate the onset of diabetic retinopathy (DR) complications. Preliminary results using a baseline algorithm (ResNet-50) on the EVIRED dataset have shown promise, indicating the potential for accurate ci-DME onset prediction through UWF-CFP (AUC = 0.73).

**Evaluation and Diverse Data Sources**
For evaluation, the DIAMOND Challenge will incorporate independent datasets from Algeria, alongside the French hospital data. This approach ensures the challenge's commitment to creating universally applicable solutions, capable of serving diverse population groups and settings.

**Methodological Challenge**
The DIAMOND Challenge introduces a significant methodological challenge that sets it apart from typical predictive modeling competitions. Participants in this challenge will not have access to the training, validation, or test datasets and, consequently, will not have the opportunity to train their models directly. Instead, they are required to submit their code as a Zip file, which the organizing committee will then run on a specialized cloud-based cluster. This methodology not only challenges participants to develop highly generalizable models but also prepares them for real-world situations where data privacy, ethical considerations, and logistical limitations are common.

description: This competition is a part of the shared task hosted within the 4th workshop on Scholarly Document Processing (SDP 2024), held in association with The 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics ACL 2024. A big problem with the ubiquity of Generative AI is that it has now become very easy to generate fake scientific papers. This can erode public trust in science and attack the foundations of science: are we standing on the shoulders of robots? The Detecting Automatically Generated Papers (DAGPap) competition aims to encourage the development of robust, reliable AI-generated scientific text detection systems, utilizing a diverse dataset and varied machine learning models in a number of scientific domains. As a follow-up to DAGPap 2022, which targeted sentence-level classification into human-written or ML-generated texts, we now extend the task to token-level classification of scientific texts into 4 classes: human-written, synonym-replaced, chatGPT-generated and summarized.

title: MICCAI CL-Detection2024: Cephalometric Landmark Detection in Lateral X-ray Images
description:
Cephalometric analysis is a fundamental examination which is routinely used in fields of orthodontics and orthognathics. The key operation in the analysis is marking craniofacial landmarks from lateral cephalograms. These landmarks serve as the datum of the succeeding qualitative assessment of angles and distances, which provide diagnosis information of the craniofacial condition of a patient and affect treatment planning decision. However, reliable landmark annotations often require experienced doctors, and even for seasoned orthodontists, manually identifying these landmarks can be a time-consuming and labor-intensive process. Hence, fully automatic and accurate landmark localization has been a long-standing area with a great deal of need.
 
 In this challenge, we aim to promote the development of universal cephalometric landmark detection in lateral X-ray images. Specifically, the detection algorithm is expected to accurately locate 53 landmarks (13 soft tissue-related landmarks, 6 tooth-related landmarks, 19 skull-related landmarks, 13 cervical spine-related landmarks, 2 calibration ruler landmarks) in lateral X-ray images. Our challenge aims to provide a comprehensive benchmark for cephalometric landmark detection methods.

title: NSF HDR iHARP: Detecting Sea Level Rise Anomalies
description:
Sea level observations from ocean buoys along the US East Coast are essential for monitoring activities and have significant societal impacts. These buoys, equipped with advanced instruments, provide continuous real-time data on tidal variations, storm surges, and long-term sea level trends. This data is transmitted via satellite to shore-based stations, offering detailed records crucial for predicting and monitoring coastal flooding, a major threat to coastal communities. Understanding storm surges and long-term sea level rise helps in issuing timely warnings, preparing for severe weather events, and implementing coastal protection measures to combat erosion.

The information gathered from these buoys also plays a vital role in ensuring maritime safety and supporting navigation for commercial and recreational vessels. Accurate sea level data are necessary for maintaining and planning maritime infrastructure, such as harbors and ports. Additionally, long-term sea level records are invaluable for studying climate change impacts, providing evidence of global warming effects like melting polar ice and thermal expansion of seawater. These observations support the resilience and sustainability of coastal economies, which rely heavily on tourism, fishing, and shipping industries. Moreover, real-time data enable quick response to emergencies, such as tsunamis or storm surges, thus reducing the risk to human lives and property and ensuring the safety and sustainability of coastal regions along the US East Coast.

Predicting sea level anomaly events, such as extreme storm surges or unusually high tides, is challenging along the low-lying US east coast region due to the complex interplay of atmospheric, oceanic, and climatic factors. These events are influenced by a combination of wind patterns, atmospheric pressure changes, and ocean currents, making accurate forecasting difficult with traditional methods. However, modern machine learning tools have the potential to enhance prediction capabilities by analyzing vast datasets from various sources, identifying patterns, and improving the accuracy of forecasts. Machine learning algorithms can process real-time data from NDBC buoys, historical sea level records, and meteorological information to provide more reliable predictions of extreme sea level events, thereby improving preparedness and mitigating the impacts on coastal communities.

title: The Algonauts Project 2025 Challenge
description:
Overview
# Welcome to The Algonauts Project 2025 Challenge Competition Page!

The goal of this Challenge is to provide a platform where biological and artificial intelligence scientists can cooperate and compete in developing cutting-edge encoding models of neural responses to multimodal naturalistic movies that well generalize outside of their training distribution. The Challenge is based on [CNeuroMod](https://www.cneuromod.ca/), the dataset that most intensively samples single-subject functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) responses to a variety of naturalistic movies.

The 2025 Challenge consists of three phases:
* **Model building phase:** During the model building phase you will train and test your encoding models using non-overlapping movie stimuli and fMRI responses from the same distribution.
* **Model selection phase:** During the model selection phase the winning models will be chosen based on their predicted fMRI responses for out-of-distribution (OOD) movie stimuli.
* **Post-Challenge phase:** After the Challenge we will open a never-ending post-Challenge phase, which will serve as a public benchmark for evaluating encoding model predicted fMRI responses for Friends season 7 or for the OOD movies.
For more details on the Challenge you can visit the [website](http://algonauts.csail.mit.edu/), read the [preprint](link), or watch [this video](link). title: Readme2KG-old
description:
The vision of NFDI4DataScience (NFDI4DS) is to support every step of the complex and interdisciplinary research data lifecycle, including collecting/creating, processing, analyzing, publishing, archiving, and reusing resources in Data Science and Artificial Intelligence. GitHub is a popular platform for hosting and collaborating on software projects. In the context of research, authors can use GitHub repositories to share the datasets, models, and source code used in experiments described in the paper. These repositories can provide implementation details and facilitate the exploration and reproduction of research results. Each GitHub repository typically includes a README.md file, which serves as an introductory document for the project. READMEs are usually written in Markdown format and provide key information such as the project’s purpose, setup instructions, usage examples, and often links to the original research paper. To enhance the NDFI4DS-KG with information from GitHub README files, we propose the following fine-grained Named Entity Recognition task:
Participants will develop classifiers that take README files as input and output the mentions of the 10 classes in the NFDI4DS Ontology (NFDI4DSO), e.g., “programming language”, “publication”, “project”, “dataset”, “software”. A dataset with approximately 200 README.md files will be made available in IOB2 format to train the classifiers. The classifiers will be evaluated using micro and macro scores of recall, precision, and F1.

With the development of multimodal large models and the popularity of content recommendation applications, multimodal recommendation has become one of the most prominent tasks in the research community. To promote breakthroughs in this field, we organize a Multimodal Click-through Rate prediction (MM-CTR) Challenge at the WWW 2025 EReL@MIR workshop. To meet the low-latency requirements of online inference in industrial applications, we have divided the MM-CTR Challenge into two sub-tasks: Multimodal Item Embedding and Multimodal CTR Prediction. The first task centers on developing multimodal item representation  learning tailored for recommendation tasks, while the second focuses on designing CTR prediction models that effectively utilize multimodal embedding features to enhance model performance. Through in-depth exploration on these two tasks, we aim to broden the boundary of multimodal recommendation and call for solutions with practical value and insights for industrial recommender systems.

Please check out more details on the challenge website:
https://erel-mir.github.io/challenge/mmctr-track2/

description:
## Overview of PolyHope-M: Bridging Hope Speech Detection Across Multiple Languages

PolyHope-M 2025 Results Link: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/11zs__2LpOeoLvFXm1le_w6GK2TCro5Ki?usp=drive_link 

Hope is a fundamental human emotion that shapes decision-making, resilience, and social interactions. It is expressed in diverse ways, ranging from generalized optimism to specific expectations about the future. The PolyHope-M shared task at [RANLP 2025](https://ranlp.org/ranlp2025/) aims to advance the computational understanding of hope by detecting and categorizing hope-related expressions in social media texts across four languages: English, German, Spanish, and Urdu.
This shared task goes beyond traditional binary classification by introducing a nuanced multiclass classification approach, distinguishing between:

* **Generalized Hope: ** A broad sense of optimism not tied to specific outcomes.
* **Realistic Hope: **An expectation grounded in achievable goals.
* **Unrealistic Hope:** A desire for outcomes that are unlikely or impossible.
* **Not Hope:** Texts that do not express hope.

### Task description
Participants will develop NLP models to classify hope-related expressions in two subtasks:

* **Subtask 1- Binary Hope Speech Detection:** Classifying texts as Hope or Not Hope. (separate for each language)
* **Subtask 2 - Multiclass Hope Speech Detection:** Distinguishing between different types of hope expressions. (separate for each language)

The PolyHope-M dataset consists of manually annotated social media texts in four languages, ensuring high-quality training data for multilingual NLP research. Submissions will be evaluated based on precision, recall, F1-score, and accuracy, with rankings determined by macro-averaged scores.

This shared task presents an opportunity to explore emotion detection, psychological linguistics, and cross-cultural NLP, contributing to the development of more inclusive and effective AI-driven language models.

title: Global Wheat Full Semantic Segmentation
description:
**WHEAT** is a cornerstone crop of global food security, serving as a dietary 
staple for billions of people worldwide. Detailed analysis of wheat plants can help plant scientists and farmers grow healthier, more resilient, more nutritious, and more abundant wheat crops. Analyzing images of wheat in-the-field is a challenging task, due to dense, overlapping, self-similar plant structures and a highly variable appearance due to the type of wheat, the growing region, and the growth stage. 

To tackle **this global wheat challenge**, we previously assembled an 
international dataset of wheat images focusing on wheat head bounding-box 
annotations. Although counting wheat heads is an important trait, the other 
parts of the wheat plant (leaves, stems, etc.) are also important for a 
holistic characterization of a wheat plant’s condition and potential. Our 
**new global wheat dataset** and competition takes a significant step 
forward by **targeting full semantic segmentation** of wheat organs. 
Semantic segmentation enables **pixel-level classification** of plant 
components such as **leaves**, **stems**, and **spikes**. This detailed understanding can provide deeper insights into plant architecture, health, and development. 

The **Global Wheat Full Semantic Segmentation (GWFSS)** dataset comprises 
images collected by **11 institutes and universities** from diverse 
geographical regions using various imaging setups. This diversity ensures that the dataset is robust to variations in environmental conditions, genotypes, and imaging techniques. 

By participating in this competition, researchers and practitioners have the 
opportunity to develop cutting-edge models that can accurately segment wheat 
organs under diverse conditions. The outcomes of this challenge have the 
potential to revolutionize digital phenotyping in agriculture by enabling 
more precise monitoring of crop health and growth. Ultimately, these advancements can contribute to global efforts in **improving food security and fostering sustainable agricultural practices**. This structure highlights the significance of the task while connecting it to broader goals like food security and sustainability. It also emphasizes the novelty of transitioning from detection to segmentation and underscores the importance of the new dataset.

This problem manifests in personal and social interactions and popular culture, particularly in songs and television shows. Music, as a massive form of cultural expression, often perpetuates negative stereotypes about women through lyrics that objectify, sexualize, or demean them. # Disclaimer:
*The following information contains subject matter that may be sensitive to certain readers. Subjects discussed may include suicide, murder, verbal/sexual/physical abuse, stalking, and other similar material. Reader discretion is advised.*

# Task Description

In today’s modern world, many people turn to anonymous online forums when they feel as if their life is in danger. Whether it be from toxic/abusive relationships, suicidal thoughts caused by depression, or they believe someone is after to get them, there are countless examples all over the internet. Many times, these posts/comments to these forums are left unread and unchecked. We wish to create a solution to be able to flag these posts/comments based on the risk posed to the author’s life.

Type of Data: First-person Reddit posts/comments
Labels (single-label assignment):
● 0 - No risk to personal safety
● 1 - Potential future risk to personal safety
● 2 - Some immediate risk to personal safety and/or future physical harm
● 3 - Significant risk of bodily harm in the present and/or future
● 4 - Extreme immediate or near-future threat to the author’s life
We believe these labels will, as accurately as possible, display and distinguish the threat to one author’s life versus another based on first-person text they wrote.

Unlike traditional approaches that generate general-purpose, one-size-fits-all descriptions of videos, this challenge enables captions tailored to specific user-defined intentions that can test video understanding modules in capturing various aspects of the video. The distinction is crucial for improving accessibility, personalization, and adaptability in multimedia applications. General video descriptions, such as the Non-Intention-Oriented example in Figure(a), offer a broad overview of the video content but lack the specificity to address particular user needs. title: Foundation Models for Genomic Modeling and Understanding
description:
All living systems encode information in their genomic sequences. Just as Watson and Crick’s helical structure cracked the DNA code [[1]](https://www.nature.com/articles/171737a0), AI is now learning the chemical language of life to decode the regulatory grammar hidden with genomes [[2]](https://crfm.stanford.edu/report.html). Foundation models (FMs), also known as large language models (LLMs), are generative AI systems that understand and generate human language. Prominent examples like Open AI’s [ChatGPT](https://chat.openai.com/) and Google’s ‎[Gemini](https://gemini.google.com/) have already transformed nearly every sector.    The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) reported in 2024 that the number of leading FMs soared by 175% globally in just six months [[3]](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/661941a6c1d297c6ad1dfeed/Update_Paper__1_.pdf). Goldman Sachs predict FM-driven generative AI could boost global GDP by ~7% ($7tn) over the next decade [[4]](https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/articles/generative-ai-could-raise-global-gdp-by-7-percent). 

Motivated by the analogy between human language and the genome’s biological code, researchers are now training LLMs on genomic data, creating genomic foundation models (gFMs). Since genomic data is mostly unlabelled, gFMs use self-supervised pretraining to learn generalisable representations directly from raw genomic sequences without relying on human annotations. This approach reduces bias and improves downstream task performance. Importantly, well designed pretraining helps models quickly adapt to ‘few-shot’ tasks. This is particularly valuable in genomics because biologists often have limited samples (e.g., specific microRNAs or enhancers). Strong ‘zero-shot’ capabilities further enable these models to uncover previously unknown genomic patterns. The potential impact of gLMs in life sciences is substantial. McKinsey estimates that generative AI could unlock $60–$110bn annual economic value within life science industries. Echoing the latest PCAST report in the USA [[5]](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/AI-Report_Upload_29APRIL2024_SEND-2.pdf), FMs offer remarkable potential to drive new era of digital biology for supercharging scientific progress, from drug discovery and super-personalised medicine.      

In this discovery challenge, we researched and designed a set of curated genomics benchmarks for evaluating the performance of different participating gFMs and/or machine learning approaches on a variety of tasks ranging from genomic sequence prediction, structural modeling, to function inference.

We expect to use this competition as a springboard to foster an active, collaborative, interdisciplinary community in this exciting yet challenging area for cracking the code of life. In addition, we are keen on promoting the FAIR principles [[6]](https://www.go-fair.org/fair-principles/) where we encourage participants to share their methodologies, scientific insights, source code, training data, etc, to collectively promote open science.

title: LaMAR - Benchmarking Localization and Mapping for Augmented Reality
description: Localization and mapping is the foundational technology for augmented reality (AR) that enables sharing and persistence of digital content in the real world. While significant progress has been made, researchers are still mostly driven by unrealistic benchmarks not representative of real-world AR scenarios. These benchmarks are often based on small-scale datasets with low scene diversity, captured from stationary cameras, and lack other sensor inputs like inertial, radio, or depth data. Furthermore, their ground-truth (GT) accuracy is mostly insufficient to satisfy AR requirements. To close this gap, we introduce LaMAR, a new benchmark with a comprehensive capture and GT pipeline that co-registers realistic trajectories and sensor streams captured by heterogeneous AR devices in large, unconstrained scenes. To establish an accurate GT, our pipeline robustly aligns the trajectories against laser scans in a fully automated manner. As a result, we publish a benchmark dataset of diverse and large-scale scenes recorded with head-mounted and hand-held AR devices. We extend several state-of-the-art methods to take advantage of the AR-specific setup and evaluate them on our benchmark. The results offer new insights on current research and reveal promising avenues for future work in the field of localization and mapping for AR.

These captions go beyond simple visual descriptions by offering deeper insights, including the names and attributes of objects, the timing, context, outcomes of events, and other crucial details—information that cannot be gleaned from merely observing the image. Given an image, participants are required to search relevant articles in a provided external database and extract necessary information to enrich the image caption. This retrieval augmentation generation track facilitates the creation of more coherent and detailed narratives, capturing not only the visible elements but also the underlying context and significance of the scene, ultimately offering a more complete understanding of what the image represents.

However, challenges remain, such as handling abstract or ambiguous queries, improving retrieval efficiency for large-scale datasets, and ensuring robustness to linguistic variations and biases in training data. This image retrieval track aims to tackle issues of realistic information from events in real life.

description:
The objective of the task is to translate onomastic (i.e., name-related) wordplay from English to French.
Such wordplay is widely used as a rhetorical device in novels, poetry, and plays. It is widespread in classic literature, such as in Shakespeare’s characters’ names, but also in names found in modern-day works such as Pokémon, Harry Potter, Asterix, and video games. Meaningful proper names in fictional universes are often neologisms. Neologisms – that is, newly coined words – are among the most common forms of linguistic creativity. Due to their highly idiosyncratic nature, neologisms – particularly humorous ones – are challenging for both humans and machines to translate.

title: METU-CCTGS Dataset – Colorectal Cancer Tumour Grade Segmentation Benchmark
description:
Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most prevalent cancer globally, affecting over 1.8 million new cases annually. It is also the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide in terms of death rates. By 2043, the number of CRC cases is projected to reach 3.2 million globally. Due to its complex pathophysiology, CRC has several subtypes that influence prognosis and treatment response. Colon cancer biopsies, obtained through colonoscopy or surgical excision, are routinely analyzed as part of histopathological evaluations. Distinguishing between benign and malignant tumors, as well as determining the tumor grade, are critical tasks for pathologists in their daily practice. Identifying the tumor grade is crucial, as it correlates strongly with patient prognosis, with poor differentiation linked to worse outcomes, and plays a key role in determining appropriate treatment options.

In this challenge, a dataset of 103 digital histopathology whole slide images (WSI)  collected from 103 patients with varying magnifications levels will be used. WSIs were pixelwise annotated by expert pathologists into 5 classes: tumor grades 1 through 3, normal mucosa and others. The dataset contains large SVS files, and their downsized versions as well. We offer downscaled version and original SVS files as training data to the competitors.

If you want to report results on a paper that are obtained from this page please do not forget to cite our paper as well : https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405844025008473

title: NeurIPS 2025 E2LM Competition
description:
Competition Overview

Existing benchmarks have proven effective for assessing the performance of fully trained large language models. However, we find striking differences in the early training stages of small models, where benchmarks often fail to provide meaningful or discriminative signals. To explore how these differences arise, this competition tackles the challenge of designing scientific knowledge evaluation tasks specifically tailored for measuring early training progress of language models. Participants are invited to develop novel evaluation methodologies or adapt existing benchmarks to better capture performance differences among language models. To support this effort, we provide three pre-trained small models (0.5B, 1B, and 3B parameters), along with intermediate checkpoints sampled during training up to 200B tokens. All experiments and development work can be run on widely available free cloud-based GPU platforms, making participation accessible to researchers with modest hardware. Submissions will be evaluated based on three criteria: the quality of the performance signal they produce, the consistency of model rankings at 1 trillion tokens of training, and their alignment with the scientific knowledge domain. By promoting the design of tailored evaluation strategies for SLMs, this competition aims to attract a broad range of participants from around the world, including those who may not be machine learning experts or have access to dedicated GPU resources. Ultimately, this initiative seeks to make foundational LLM research more systematic and benchmark-informed from the earliest phases of model development.

Video understanding is a crucial task in that the ultimate goal is to capture everything happening in a video, and it is not the state of the ideal performance in the existing literature. Unlike traditional approaches that generate general-purpose, one-size-fits-all descriptions of videos, this challenge enables captions tailored to specific user-defined intentions that can test video understanding modules in capturing various aspects of the video. The distinction is crucial for improving accessibility, personalization, and adaptability in multimedia applications. title: CroCoDL - Cross-device Collaborative Dataset for Localization
description:
Accurate localization plays a pivotal role in the autonomy of systems operating in unfamiliar environments, particularly when interaction with humans is expected. High-accuracy visual localization systems encompass various components, such as feature extractors, matchers, and pose estimation methods. This complexity translates to the necessity of robust evaluation settings and pipelines. However, existing datasets and benchmarks primarily focus on single-agent scenarios, overlooking the critical issue of cross-device localization. Different agents with different sensors will show their own specific strengths and weaknesses, and the data they have available varies substantially. This work addresses this gap by enhancing an existing augmented reality visual localization benchmark with data from legged robots, and evaluating human-robot, cross-device mapping and localization. Our contributions extend beyond device diversity and include high environment variability, spanning ten distinct locations ranging from disaster sites to art exhibitions. Each scene in our dataset features recordings from robot agents, hand-held and head-mounted devices, and high-accuracy ground truth LiDAR scanners, resulting in a comprehensive multi-agent dataset and benchmark. This work represents a significant advancement in the field of visual localization benchmarking, with key insights into the performance of cross-device localization methods across diverse settings.

description:
Welcome to the WCLOP 2025 Challenge! This challenge is part of the 1st Workshop on Category-Level Object Pose Estimation for Robotic Manipulation, focusing on advancing category-level 6D object pose estimation in complex real-world scenarios. Unlike traditional instance-level methods that require known object meshes or reference images, our challenge addresses the more practical scenario where only object category information is available.

The WCLOP 2025 Challenge consists of **two complementary phases**:
- **Phase 1:** Category-Level Pose Estimation in Complex Real-World Scenarios
- **Phase 2:** Pose Estimation Evaluation Through Downstream Robotic Manipulation Tasks (test data to be released later in August - participants will use their Phase 1 trained models on Phase 2's test data. Stay tuned!)

**Phase 1** focuses on **Category-Level Pose Estimation in Complex Real-World Scenarios** using the **Omni6DPose** and **PACE** datasets. These datasets provide diverse object categories, challenging occlusion scenarios, articulated objects, and realistic lighting conditions that push the boundaries of current pose estimation methods for robotic manipulation applications.

This track aims to encourage participants to develop robust ESDD systems for unseen (Text-to-Audio) TTA and (Audio-to-Audio) ATA generators. The primary objective is to promote the creation of detection models that can effectively identify synthetic environmental sounds generated by unseen TTA and ATA systems. By focusing on the unseen-generator scenario, this track aims to simulate practical use cases where the source and generation models of deepfake audio are not known seen during training. We seek to advance research in generalized deepfake detection and promote the design of models with strong cross-generator robustness and adaptability.

The “low-resource” setting indicates that the amount of available black-box training data is severely limited, constituting only 1% of the total training data. Together, this track presents a realistic and challenging scenario that simulates practical deepfake detection under extreme uncertainty and data scarcity.

**Task Description**

Offensive language is a pervasive issue on social media platforms. The widespread adoption and popularity of social media platforms have amplified the spread of such harmful content. Over recent years, the presence of offensive posts has been linked to serious negative consequences, including mental health challenges such as depression and increased suicide attempts.

To address these harms, content moderation by humans has been a common approach. However, given the vast and growing volume of user-generated content, manual moderation alone is no longer feasible. This has created a pressing requirement for automated methods to detect offensive language effectively and at scale. As a result, computational approaches have become popular in offensive language detection.

Following this trend, this task invites you to build robust machine learning models capable of identifying offensive language in a multilingual setting.

This task is composed of two sub-tasks, as follows:

* Sub-task A: Post-level Offensive Language Detection - Given a social media post, this task requires assigning the label 'OFF' if it contains offensive content or 'NOT' if it does not contain any offensive content. [Link](https://www.codabench.org/competitions/10043/#/participate-tab)

title: ICASSP 2026: Radar acoustic speech enhancement (RASE) challenge (Official submission only)
description:
The RASE 2026 Challenge explores the next frontier in speech enhancement by leveraging mmWave radar as a sensing modality. Traditional microphone-based systems often fail in noisy, obstructed, or privacy-sensitive environments. Radar provides a contactless, non-intrusive alternative capable of capturing rich motion and articulation cues through physical barriers such as glass.
Participants are tasked with developing models that reconstruct clean and intelligible speech signals from radar echoes recorded across varying environments, user orientations, and glass conditions. This is a highly interdisciplinary challenge at the intersection of signal processing, machine learning, and wireless sensing.
We provide a curated dataset of paired radar–audio signals for training. Models will be evaluated on held-out test data using a combination of objective speech quality and intelligibility metrics, including PESQ, ESTOI, DNSMOS, MFCC similarity, and a final weighted score. Leaderboards will track performance across phases, encouraging both innovation and reproducibility.
The ultimate goal of RASE 2026 is to benchmark state-of-the-art methods, foster collaboration between the radar and speech research communities, and pave the way for real-world applications in healthcare, security, and human–machine interaction.

title: ARHAHA 2026 :  Arabic Humor Automatic Generation Shared Task
description:
Humor understanding has attracted increasing attention in recent NLP research; however, the automatic generation of humorous content remains a particularly challenging problem, especially for underrepresented languages such as Arabic. Humor generation requires not only linguistic fluency, but also cultural awareness, creativity, and the ability to surprise while remaining socially appropriate.

ARHAHA 2026 is a shared task dedicated to Arabic humor generation, aiming to provide a structured evaluation framework for studying creative language generation in Arabic. The task focuses on encouraging systems to produce original, safe, and culturally grounded humorous texts, rather than reproducing memorized jokes.

Despite the richness and diversity of Arabic linguistic and cultural traditions, there is currently no standardized benchmark for Arabic humor generation. ARHAHA addresses this gap by introducing carefully designed constraints and evaluation protocols that promote novelty and fairness, while allowing meaningful comparison between systems.

Participants are invited to develop models that generate short humorous texts in Arabic under explicit constraints. Evaluation combines automatic validation of format and constraints with human assessment of humor quality, originality, fluency, and cultural appropriateness.

The task aims to advance research on creative language generation for Arabic and has potential applications in conversational agents, entertainment-oriented AI, educational tools, and culturally aware human–computer interaction.

More details about the task, data, and participation instructions are available at: https://sites.google.com/view/arhaha2026/home

description: The task investigates politeness in Arabic social‑media posts, a pragmatic phenomenon that affects how people perceive and respond to messages. In Arabic the concept is deeply rooted in cultural norms; speakers employ honorifics, plural forms of address and kinship terms to show respect. Most computational work on politeness focuses on English, with only limited studies on other languages. For Arabic, there is no extensive public dataset available, and researchers often have to depend on small, limited datasets.

Three previous editions of PARSEME shared tasks ([1.0](https://aclanthology.org/W17-1704.pdf), [1.1](https://aclanthology.org/W18-4925.pdf), [1.2](https://aclanthology.org/2020.mwe-1.14.pdf)) were dedicated to identification of MWEs, but have focused on verbal MWEs only. We propose here to deal with all syntactic categories of MWEs. Additionally, we deal with paraphrasing MWEs, which is closer to understanding than sheer identification. We propose two subtasks. The first corresponds to the classical identification task in running text. The second consists in paraphrasing a sentence containing a MWE, so as to remove idiomaticity. This Codabench competition is the implementation of **subtask 2 - MWE paraphrasing**.

title: Shared Task on Understanding Toxic Behavioral Intent in Gaming Chat Logs@EEUCA with ACL 2026
description: Online gaming communities thrive on fast-paced interaction and competition, but they also face persistent challenges from toxic behavior that can negatively impact player experience and safety. This shared task is built on the GameTox dataset, a large-scale collection of over 53K real-world game chat utterances annotated for toxicity intent classification. The challenge invites participants to develop models that can accurately detect harmful intent in highly dynamic, informal, and adversarial conversational settings typical of gaming platforms. By focusing on intent-level understanding rather than surface-level keyword matching, this task encourages the development of more robust, context-aware, and interpretable toxicity detection systems. Ultimately, the shared task aims to advance scalable moderation technologies that can help foster healthier and safer online gaming environments.

title: Shared Task on Multimodal Identification of Vaccine Critical Content on Social Media@EEUCA with ACL 2026
description: Memes have become a powerful and fast-spreading medium for sharing information online, especially around high-impact public health issues such as COVID-19 vaccination. While memes can be used to promote awareness and positive behavior, they are also frequently used to spread misinformation, skepticism, and vaccine-critical narratives, often through sarcasm and implicit context that make automated analysis challenging. This shared task is based on the VaxMeme dataset, a collection of over 10,000 manually annotated vaccination-related memes, designed to support multimodal vaccine-critical meme detection. The task invites participants to develop models that jointly leverage both visual and textual representations to capture the global and local contextual cues embedded in memes. By focusing on fine-grained multimodal understanding, this challenge aims to advance more reliable systems for monitoring vaccine-related discourse, supporting myth debunking efforts, and informing the design of effective public health communication strategies on social media platforms.

title: Subtask A(Hate Detection) for Shared Task on Multimodal Hate and Sentiment Understanding in Low-Resource Memes@CHiPSAL LREC 2026
description: Memes in low-resource languages such as Nepali play an increasingly important role in online discourse, yet they remain significantly underrepresented in multimodal research. This shared task focuses on multimodal hate detection in Nepali memes, where each meme is annotated as hate or no-hate. The task challenges participants to develop models that can effectively integrate visual and textual cues to detect harmful content in a low-resource linguistic setting marked by cultural context, code-mixing, sarcasm, and informal language. By addressing the scarcity of annotated resources and benchmarks for Nepali, this challenge aims to push forward fair, inclusive, and robust multimodal hate detection systems that generalize beyond high-resource languages.

title: Subtask B(Sentiment Analysis) for Shared Task on Multimodal Hate and Sentiment Understanding in Low-Resource Memes@CHiPSAL LREC 2026
description: Understanding sentiment in memes goes beyond identifying positive or negative words, as meaning often emerges from the interaction between images, text, and cultural context. This shared task targets multimodal sentiment analysis in low-resource Nepali memes, where each meme is labelled as positive, negative, or neutral. Participants are invited to explore how joint visual-textual representations can improve sentiment recognition in noisy, culturally rich, and resource-scarce environments. By focusing on Nepali, this challenge encourages the development of language-inclusive and context-aware sentiment models, contributing toward more equitable sentiment analysis technologies for global social media platforms.

title: FoodBench-QA: Shared Task on Grounded Food & Nutrition Question Answering
description:
FoodBench-QA 2025 addresses a critical gap in today’s AI ecosystem: the mismatch between general-purpose language models and the specialized knowledge required for food and nutrition applications. This shared task challenges systems to generate accurate, evidence-grounded answers to realistic dietary and recipe-related questions by leveraging structured food databases, measurement standards, and domain ontologies.

The dataset is designed around the core difficulties that make the food domain uniquely complex—ambiguous ingredient terminology, non-standard and variable measurements, heterogeneous nutritional sources, and the need for precise entity disambiguation. Participants evaluate their models across three complementary tasks: nutrient estimation for recipes, FSA traffic-light prediction, and food-specific NER/NEL. Each task is paired with domain-appropriate evaluation metrics aligned with regulatory guidelines to ensure reliable and interpretable performance.

title: AdabEval 2026:  Arabic Politeness Detection Shared Task (Task B)
description:
The task investigates politeness in Arabic social‑media posts, a pragmatic phenomenon that affects how people perceive and respond to messages. Politeness plays a central role in conversation, languages provide diverse ways to encode respect and reduce imposition, and these markers are intimately tied to social power and interpersonal harmony. In Arabic the concept is deeply rooted in cultural norms; speakers employ honorifics, plural forms of address and kinship terms to show respect. Most computational work on politeness focuses on English, with only limited studies on other languages. For Arabic, there is no extensive public dataset available, and researchers often have to depend on small, limited datasets.

This subtask evaluates the ability of systems to identify multiple pragmatic functions in Arabic social-media posts. Each text may express one or more categories from nine culturally grounded functions such as criticism, insult, respect, prayer, greeting, or hospitality. The task is framed as multi-label classification, and systems must predict all applicable categories for each instance. The official evaluation metric is macro-averaged F1-score across the nine categories.

description:
# GRACE: Granular Recognition of Argumentative Clinical Evidence

Welcome to the **GRACE** shared task, hosted at **IberLEF 2026**.

As Artificial Intelligence becomes more integrated into healthcare, the "Black Box" nature of Deep Learning models remains a barrier to clinical adoption. The GRACE task addresses this by focusing on **Argument Mining (AM)** in the medical domain. Our goal is to move beyond simple predictions and toward **Explainable AI (XAI)** by automatically identifying the evidence and reasoning structures that support clinical decisions.

GRACE is the first Argument Mining task in Spanish to address two distinct, high-stakes contexts: **Clinical Trials** and **Medical Licensing Examinations**.

### 🚀 Task Tracks

Participants can choose to engage in one or both of the following tracks:

#### Track 1: Clinical Trial Evidence & Argumentation

This track focuses on the reporting of scientific evidence within abstracts of **Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs)**. Because RCTs compare interventions against controls under strict methodology, they provide a transparent path from data to conclusions.

* **Goal**: Identify argumentative components (claims and premises) and detect the logical relations (support or attack) that connect them at the sentence level.

#### Track 2: Clinical Case Reasoning (MIR)

This track shifts focus to active clinical decision-making using cases from the **MIR (Médico Interno Residente)** exams—the national standardized test for medical specialization in Spain.

* **Goal**: Process dense clinical narratives to extract specific "spans" of evidence that justify a correct diagnosis or treatment plan while refuting incorrect alternatives.

title: Toy_benchmark_v1
description:
## Toy Benchmark v1: Pairwise Point Tracking

This benchmark evaluates a simple **pairwise point tracking** task on image data.

### Task Definition
For each test sample, participants are given:
- A reference image (`ref`)
- A target image (`tgt`)
- A reference point `(x_ref, y_ref)` defined on the reference image

The goal is to **predict the corresponding point location `(x, y)` on the target image**.

### Evaluation
Predictions are evaluated using the **Euclidean distance** between the predicted point and the ground-truth point on the target image.
The final score is the **mean error over all test samples** (lower is better).

title: NTIRE 2026 Real-World Face Restoration
description:
The 2nd NTIRE Real-World Face Restoration Challenge, in conjunction with CVPR 2026. https://ntire-face.github.io/2026/

Face restoration aims to recover high-quality (HQ) face images from degraded low-quality (LQ) inputs affected by blur, noise, compression, and other distortions, making it a highly ill-posed problem. Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved face restoration. While traditional methods focused on explicit facial priors and degradation modeling, modern approaches leveraging CNNs, Transformers, and generative models (e.g., diffusion model) have demonstrated superior performance.


NTIRE workshop aims to provide an overview of the new trends and advances in those areas. Moreover, it will offer an opportunity for academic and industrial attendees to interact and explore collaborations.

As part of the NTIRE 2025 workshop, this challenge focuses on restoring high-quality (HQ) face images from degraded low-quality (LQ) inputs. The aim is to develop a network design/solution that achieves high-quality restoration results with the best performance on perceptual quality.

title: 8th UG2+ Challenge (CVPR 2026) Track 2: Semantic Segmentation In Adverse Weather
description: The competition will feature diverse and challenging scenarios that include (i) various types of weather conditions, e.g. light and heavy degrees of rain, snow, and fog, (ii) large variety of background scenes from urban locations (i.e. buildings, streets, cityscapes) to natural scenery (i.e. forests, plains, hills), (iii) varying degrees of illumination from different times of day, and all of which are captured by (iv) cameras that cover a wide array of resolutions, noise levels, and intrinsic parameters. The goal of the challenge is to spark innovative and robust approaches for semantic segmentation under adverse conditions. To this end, the challenge will be split into two phases (training and testing), where data corresponding to each phase will be released to the participants. The submissions will be evaluated quantitatively using standard metrics like mean intersection-over-union (mIOU) and similarity coefficient (mDICE). Participants will submit their results on the testing set for evaluation, with a limited number of attempts per phase to ensure fairness amongst teams registering for the competition at different times. The best results for each phase will be reported on the benchmark. The ranking of algorithms will be determined based on evaluation scores on the testing set. Participants are required to submit a fact sheet including description of their method, datasets used, hyperparameters, memory, runtime, and hardware requirements, etc. The fact sheets will be compiled into a final report post challenge to highlight trends and innovations. Participants are encouraged to submit manuscripts detailing their method to the workshop.

**Challenge Overview**


Images captured in adverse weather conditions significantly impact the performance of many vision tasks. Common weather phenomena include rain, snow and fog that introduces visual degradations to captured images and videos. As most vision algorithms assume clear weather, with no interference of weather conditions, their performance suffers. De-weathering aims to remove such visual degradations so that the images are better suited to the assumptions of downstream vision algorithms, as well as for aesthetic fruition. This track will feature, WeatherStream, a dataset of 136.9K time-multiplexed real images pairs collected under adverse weather conditions.

Predict Trade in Value Added (TiVA) flows between countries using macroeconomic indicators.

**Context**: In today's globalized economy, understanding how value is created and distributed across international supply chains is crucial. - TiVA data from OECD covering 2005-2020

- Public test set (2018): For leaderboard ranking during the competition
- Private test set (2019): For final ranking after competition closure

title: Directional Forecasting of the S&P 500 Index
description:
Can you predict whether the S&P 500 will close UP or DOWN tomorrow?
Each trading day, participants receive a historical feature vector built from past daily OHLCV data (Open, High, Low, Close, Volume) of the S&P 500 index.
The target label is binary: **1** if the next trading day's close is strictly above the current day's close, **0** otherwise. Participants are encouraged to engineer their own historical context features (e.g., rolling volatility, moving averages) using the provided sequential data.
Participants submit a PyTorch model via a `submission.py` file exposing a `get_model(train_loader)` function. The ingestion program passes a `DataLoader` yielding `(x, y)` batches where:
  - `x` is a `FloatTensor` of shape `(batch, WINDOW_SIZE, n_features)` — a sliding window of historical daily features
  - `y` is a `FloatTensor` of shape `(batch,)` — binary labels (1 = up, 0 = down)

`get_model` must return a trained `torch.nn.Module` whose forward pass accepts a tensor of shape `(batch, WINDOW_SIZE, n_features)` and returns **probabilities in [0, 1]** of shape `(batch,)`.
Submissions are ranked by their **ROC-AUC** score computed from the predicted probabilities.
This is a DataCamp challenge organised at École Polytechnique (INF554 / MAP583).

title: Inshorts Short News Topic Classification
description:
# Overview

This competition focuses on **single-label topic classification for short English news articles**.

Each instance consists of:
- a **news headline**
- a **short news article summary**

The goal is to predict exactly **one topic label** for each instance from the following 7 categories:

- `technology`
- `sports`
- `politics`
- `entertainment`
- `world`
- `automobile`
- `science`

This task is based on short-form news data from the **Inshorts** news dataset. Compared with long-form news articles, short summaries provide less context, so models must identify the main topic from a brief and information-dense input. Some categories can also overlap semantically, such as **science vs. technology** or **technology vs. automobile**, which makes the task more challenging.

This is a **supervised multiclass text classification** task. The input is formed by concatenating the headline and article summary into a single text sequence, and the output is one categorical topic label.

The main evaluation metrics are:

- **Accuracy**
- **Macro-F1**

Accuracy measures overall correctness, while Macro-F1 gives equal importance to each class and helps evaluate performance more fairly across all categories.

title: RECoDe - Relation Extraction for Diet, Non-Communicable Disease and Biomarker Associations: A CoDiet study
description:
The RECoDe relation extraction benchmark focuses on identifying semantic relationships between pairs of biomedical entities in the context of diet, non-communicable diseases, and related bio-entities. The dataset captures 10 relation types, covering a diverse spectrum of interactions, including positive associations, directional effects, compositional relations, and explicit negative cases.

These relation types are:
- association
- increaseAssociation
- decreaseAssociation
- positiveCorrelation
- negativeCorrelation
- consists
- causalEffect
- substitution
- NoAssociation
- Unrelated

Participants are required to automatically predict the relation type between a given pair of entities based on the provided textual context. Each instance corresponds to a candidate entity pair extracted from biomedical documents.

description:
Misogyny – understood as any form of discrimination, prejudice, or aversion towards women based on their gender – is a deeply rooted global issue spanning generations. The consequences women face due to misogyny include gender-based violence, economic inequalities, social exclusion, mental health issues, and unequal access to education and job opportunities.

This problem manifests in personal and social interactions and popular culture, particularly in songs and television shows. Music, as a massive form of cultural expression, often perpetuates negative stereotypes about women through lyrics that objectify, sexualize, or demean them. This directly influences how society normalizes such behaviors and reinforces misogynistic attitudes. Similarly, television programs and content frequently portray women in subordinate, hypersexualized roles or as two-dimensional characters, contributing to the perpetuation of gender biases and inequality.

title: PAN-CLEF 2026 - Subtask 1: Source Detection
description:
The year 2025 saw major advances in the reasoning capabilities of large language models, where models produce explicit reasoning trajectories before a final answer. However, intermediate reasoning steps can still be spurious, non-logical, or unsafe, and in some cases models may reach safe conclusions through deceptive or misaligned reasoning paths. To deepen our understanding of LLM-generated reasoning and to support improvements in reasoning and safety, this task focuses on detecting the source and the safety of reasoning trajectories.

**Subtask 1: Source Detection**
Given a triplet (user query, reasoning trajectory, final answer), identify whether the reasoning trajectory and final answer are generated by an AI system or written by a human. Queries in the testing set may involve math, coding, and real-life financial reasoning tasks.
**Total Samples:**
**Training set:** 87,696
**Validation set:** 497
**Domain:** Math from various level of difficulty and complexity.
**Generators:** K2-Think V2, GPT-5 Nano, Gemini-3 Flash, DeepSeek R1.
**Dataset Fields:**
* problem: The math problem. It may varies from basic problems, practical problems to Olympiad-level problems.
* solution: The solution of the given problem. The solution is reformated in
* generator: The author of the solution. It could be human or llm.
* detailed_generator: It could be human or name of the generated LLM.

**For more information and to download the data**, please refer to our [official GitHub repository](https://github.com/mbzuai-nlp/PAN-CLEF2026-Reasoning-Trajectory-Detection).

**Submission Format:**
Participants must submit a csv file named **submission.csv** with the following columns:
* ID (String): Sample ID matching the test set (e.g s1_000001)
* label (String): Your predicted source (human or ai, case insensitive)
There's also a sample submission.csv in the starter kit
**Evaluation metrics:**
Your rankings are evaluated using macro F1 Score as the primary metric:
For each class (human and ai), F1 is computed as:
F1= (2 x Precision x Recall)/(Precision+Recall)
Macro F1 = ( F1(human)+F1(AI) )/2



Given a triplet (user query, reasoning trajectory, final answer), identify whether the reasoning trajectory and final answer are generated by an AI system or written by a human. Queries in the testing set may involve math, coding, and real-life financial reasoning tasks.

title: SatiSPeech 2025 Task
description: Satire is a complex and multifaceted form of communication that combines humor, irony, and criticism to expose or ridicule social, political, or cultural issues. Unlike straightforward humor, satire often relies on subtle cues such as tone, exaggeration, or context, making it difficult for even humans to identify and interpret. This difficulty is compounded in multimodal contexts, where meaning can emerge from the interplay of text, speech, and prosodic elements. Misinterpretation of satire can lead to misunderstandings or unintended consequences, especially when it addresses sensitive issues or employs sharp criticism. Despite these challenges, enabling machines to recognize and interpret satire is increasingly valuable for applications such as media analysis, misinformation detection, and sentiment understanding. Using multimodal approaches that combine textual, acoustic, and contextual signals, it is possible to advance the development of systems capable of capturing the nuanced and context-dependent nature of satire.

title: EmoSPeech 2024 Task - Multimodal Speech-text Emotion Recognition in Spanish
description: Recognizing human emotions is crucial for building positive relationships, whether it is in person or through interactions with computers (Varghese, Cherian, y Kizhakkethottam, 2015). Automatic Emotion Recognition (AER) has been a significant problem for many years, and its importance is growing due to its impact on various fields such as healthcare, psychology, social sciences, and marketing (Chenchah y Lachiri, 2016; Lugovic, Dunder, y Horvat, 2016). In the software domain, AER can help provide more personalized responses and recommendations, leading to improved user engagement and satisfaction. The process of AER can be addressed using several taxonomies the most popular being the recognition of six basic emotional expressions, which are anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, and surprise (Ekman, 1992). By automatically recognizing emotions, a system can identify, interpret, and respond to emotions expressed by humans in various communication channels, such as text, facial expressions, voice tones, or even body language. Different features can be used to identify emotions, such as language features, voice intonation, intensity, duration, or even the conversational rhythm (Fahad et al., 2021). These features can be integrated into a multimodal paradigm that combines different types of data, such as text and speech, to achieve higher performance.

title: IBERLEF 2023 Task - FinancES. Financial Targeted Sentiment Analysis in Spanish
description: The need to manage financial data has been increasingly coming into sharp focus for some time (Hasan et al., 2020). Years ago, these data sat in warehouses attached to specific applications in banks and financial companies. Then the Web came into the arena, facilitating the access to economic, financial and monetary data. With vast amounts of financial information posted online, there are ample opportunities to monitor public opinion, receive early warnings and perform positive and negative impact analysis. The effects of emotions on financial markets have been demonstrated in several studies (Goodell et al., 2022; Nemes & Kiss, 2021). However, different factors hamper the effectiveness of sentiment analysis in the financial domain. First, financial language is inherently complex since financial terms refer to an underlying social, economic and legal context (Milne & Chisholm, 2013). Furthermore, the type of language used within this domain is highly dependent on the context since one word or expression may have either positive or negative connotations depending on the context where it is used (stock market shares rise, debt rises, etc.). Finally, the degree of subjectivity within the financial domain is not hard to determine, because an event can be deemed positive or negative depending on the point of view. For instance, there are financial news which are positive for banks and very negative for the society or for any other business sector.

title: PAN-CLEF 2026 - Subtask 2: Safety Detection
description:
# Subtask 2 — Safety Detection

Given a triplet *(user query, reasoning trajectory, final answer)*, classify:

1. Whether each reasoning step is safe or unsafe
2. Whether the overall reasoning trace is safe or unsafe

The user queries come from three categories:

* Risky queries requesting harmful content
* Jailbreak attacks with hidden risks
* Benign queries containing risky tokens

---

# Data

## Total Samples

* Training set: 6,079
* Validation set: 2,200

---

# Dataset Fields

### generator

The model used to generate the reasoning trace.

### reasoning_trace

The segmented reasoning trace using the format:

```text
Step 1: ...
Step 2: ...
```

### label

Overall label for the reasoning trace.

Possible values:

* `safe`
* `potentially unsafe`
* `unsafe`

### detailed_label

Binary label for each reasoning step.

Values:

* `0` = safe
* `1` = unsafe

**Note:**
Some reasoning steps may be unsafe while the overall reasoning trace is safe, and vice versa.

---

# Submission Format

Participants must submit a CSV file named:

```text
submission.csv
```

with the following columns:

| Column         | Description                                        |
| -------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| ID             | Sample ID matching the test set                    |
| label          | Overall reasoning trace label (`safe` or `unsafe`) |
| detailed_label | Pipe-separated binary per-step labels              |

Example:

```text
ID,label,detailed_label
s2_000001,safe,1|0|1|1
```

---

# detailed_label Rules

* Each value corresponds to one reasoning step
* Only binary values are accepted:

  * `0` = safe
  * `1` = unsafe

Example:

```text
1|0|1|1
```

If the number of predicted steps differs from the ground truth:

* Predictions are truncated or padded during evaluation
* Missing prediction steps are treated as `0`

---

# Evaluation Metrics

Two metrics are reported.

## 1. s2_f1 — Macro F1 on overall label

* Binary classification:

  * `safe`
  * `unsafe`

* F1 is computed independently for each class and macro-averaged

* This is the primary ranking metric

---

## 2. s2_reasoning_f1 — Weighted per-sample F1 on detailed_label

For each sample:

1. Binary F1 is computed between predicted and ground-truth reasoning-step labels
2. Each sample is weighted by its number of reasoning steps
3. Final score is the weighted average across all samples

Per-sample F1:

```text
F1 = 2*TP / (2*TP + FP + FN)
```

where:

* TP = predicted unsafe step that is truly unsafe
* FP = predicted unsafe step that is actually safe
* FN = missed unsafe step

Final weighted score:

```text
weighted_mean(F1_i, number_of_steps_i)
```

Missing prediction steps are treated as `0`.

---

# Starter Kit

Included in the starter kit:

* Sample `submission.csv`
* Example prediction format
* Evaluation script

---

# Data

Dataset files are provided separately in the competition resources.

title: EuMINe DataBridge Hackaton 2026 - Step 1
description:
Teams must predict two correlated properties of inorganic crystalline materials:

Formation energy per atom (eV/atom) — thermodynamic stability
Electronic band gap (eV) — electronic/optical character
These properties are chosen because:

Both are available in multiple public databases, enabling genuine multi-source integration
They have different prediction difficulties (formation energy: well-studied; band gap: harder, DFT-underestimated)
They are inter-related (stability affects electronic structure), rewarding physics-informed approaches
They are industrially and scientifically relevant (energy materials, semiconductors, catalysts)

The Data Landscape
Participants must work with at least two of the following open sources:

Source	Type	Access	Notes
Materials Project	DFT (PBE)	REST API / bulk download	~150k entries with both properties
AFLOW	DFT (various)	REST API / aflowlib	~3.5M entries, different PAW settings
NOMAD	DFT / experiment	REST API	Repository with diverse methods
OQMD	DFT (PBE)	REST API / download	~1M entries, good coverage
JARVIS-DFT	DFT (OptB88vdW)	Download	Special focus on 2D and van der Waals
ICSD (open portion)	Experimental structures	Download	Crystal structures without properties
Organizers will provide:

A curated "Bridge Dataset" (~800 materials): a subset where all five sources have entries for the same material, with documented discrepancies and cross-references. This is the core integration challenge.
A fixed test set (held-out, never released) for final evaluation.
A train/validation split suggestion.

The Federation Angle
Each team's submitted model must implement a standardized prediction interface (MatFed API v1), defined by the organizers. This is a simple Python function signature + JSON I/O schema (see Section 6).

Organizers will run a post-submission federation experiment: they will ensemble all qualified team models using a simple stacking/weighting approach and evaluate whether the combined model outperforms individual models. Teams whose models contribute positively to the federation are scored additionally.

This models exactly what would happen in a real EuMINe data integration initiative.

title: EBMV 2026 @ ECCV - Event-Guided Brightness Adjustment on SEE-600K
description:
# EBMV 2026 Low-Level Imaging Challenge: Event-Guided Brightness Adjustment on SEE-600K

## Overview

Real-world images often suffer from different lighting degradations, including low light, over-exposure, mixed illumination, and high-contrast scenes. This challenge aims to study a unified event-guided solution for low-level image enhancement under broad lighting conditions.

Participants are asked to use RGB frames and event data to recover clear, well-exposed, and structurally faithful images. The challenge is associated with the ECCV 2026 Workshop on Event-Based Multimodal Vision: Imaging, Perception, and Understanding.

## Dataset

This challenge is based on SEE-600K, introduced in:

“SEE: See Everything Every Time - Adaptive Brightness Adjustment for Broad Light Range Images via Events”

SEE-600K is a large-scale RGB-event dataset collected under diverse lighting conditions and real-world scenarios. It provides paired RGB images and event data for event-guided brightness adjustment and low-level image restoration.

Dataset:
https://huggingface.co/datasets/yunfanlu/SEE-600K

Baseline code:
https://github.com/yunfanLu/SEE

Workshop website:
https://eventbasemultimodalvision.github.io

## Task

Participants need to develop an event-guided low-level imaging model.

Input:
1. An RGB image captured under challenging illumination.
2. The corresponding event stream or event representation.
3. Optional metadata or exposure prompt, if provided.

Output:
1. A brightness-adjusted RGB image.
2. The output should preserve scene structure, recover useful details, and avoid unrealistic hallucination.

The task focuses on event-guided brightness adjustment and image enhancement, rather than general image generation.

## Challenge Track

### Broad-Light Adaptive Brightness Adjustment

Participants are encouraged to train models on SEE-600K. Extra training data is allowed, but all external datasets, collection settings, and pretrained models should be clearly reported in the final technical report.

## Submission Format

Each submission should be uploaded as a compressed ZIP file.

Recommended structure:

submission.zip
├── scene_000001.png
├── scene_000002.png
├── scene_000003.png
└── ...

Requirements:
1. The output filename must match the input sample ID.
2. Images should be saved as PNG files.
3. Output images should be RGB images.
4. The output resolution must be the same as the input/reference resolution.
5. Do not change the file names or folder structure.
6. Do not include extra files unless explicitly required.

## Evaluation

The official evaluation will be conducted on the test set.

Metrics:
1. PSNR: pixel-level reconstruction accuracy.
2. SSIM: structural similarity.
3. LPIPS: perceptual similarity.

Ranking:
1. PSNR is the primary ranking metric.
2. SSIM and LPIPS will be used as secondary metrics.
3. The final leaderboard will be based on the official test set.

The validation server is mainly for development and submission-format checking.

## Important Dates

May 15, 2026: Challenge website opens.

May 25, 2026: Validation server online.

June 25, 2026: Test data released and test server online.

July 3, 2026: Test submission deadline and test server closes.

July 10, 2026: Results announcement. Tentative.

## Awards

Top teams will be recognized at the ECCV 2026 Workshop on Event-Based Multimodal Vision.

## Citation

If you use SEE-600K or the SEE baseline, please cite:

“SEE: See Everything Every Time - Adaptive Brightness Adjustment for Broad Light Range Images via Events”

More information is available at:
https://github.com/yunfanLu/SEE

title: AraGenre: A Hierarchical Definition-Guided Arabic Genre Classification Shared Task
description:
AraGenre: A Hierarchical Definition-Guided Arabic Genre Classification Shared Task

AraGenre is a shared task on hierarchical Arabic genre classification. The task evaluates whether systems can identify the communicative genre of Arabic texts across two levels of granularity:

  • Broad Genre: a high-level communicative function category such as Informative, Interactive, Creative, Religious, Legal, or Learning.
  • Specific Genre: a finer-grained communicative subtype within a broad category, such as analytical reports, encyclopaedic writing, motivational writing, diplomatic communication, religious commentary, forum discussions, or educational explanations.

For example:

  • Broad Genre: Informative → Specific Genre: Encyclopaedic Writing
  • Broad Genre: Interactive → Specific Genre: Forum Discussion
  • Broad Genre: Religious → Specific Genre: Religious Commentary
  • Broad Genre: Learning → Specific Genre: Educational Explanation

Unlike traditional text classification benchmarks that rely primarily on large annotated datasets and stable training distributions, AraGenre focuses on robust genre understanding across diverse communicative settings, dialects, orthographic conventions, and writing styles.

AraGenre treats genre as a discourse- and function-oriented phenomenon shaped by communicative intent, rhetorical structure, stylistic organisation, and social purpose rather than topical vocabulary alone. Systems are therefore encouraged to model transferable communicative and stylistic characteristics rather than rely solely on lexical overlap.

The shared task adopts a definition-guided evaluation framework. Participants are provided with:

  • a hierarchical Arabic genre taxonomy,
  • textual definitions describing each genre category,
  • labelled training and development data,
  • and a hidden evaluation benchmark containing naturally occurring Arabic texts.

The genre definitions are intentionally provided in English rather than Arabic. This reflects a realistic setting commonly encountered in multilingual and low-resource NLP research, where task definitions, annotation guidelines, ontologies, and metadata are frequently available primarily in English while the target texts belong to another language. Systems must therefore learn to connect English genre definitions with Arabic textual realisations across different communicative settings.

The released training and development sets consist of synthetic and carefully controlled examples designed to simulate low-resource conditions where only limited labelled data are available. In contrast, the hidden evaluation benchmark contains substantially noisier naturally occurring texts collected from diverse communicative settings and linguistic environments.

The hidden evaluation setup additionally introduces genre-definition combinations and linguistic variation that do not explicitly appear in the released training data. Systems must therefore rely on semantic understanding of genre definitions and communicative function rather than memorisation of narrow label-specific patterns.

The benchmark spans Modern Standard Arabic, Classical Arabic, and multiple Arabic dialects, including both formal and informal writing styles as well as diacritised and undiacritised text.

Systems are evaluated separately at the broad and specific genre levels. The official ranking metric is Hierarchical Macro F1, calculated as the average of:

  • Broad Macro F1
  • Specific Macro F1

While the task adopts the term “genre” in a broad computational and functional sense, the organisers acknowledge that some categories may overlap with neighbouring notions in linguistics and discourse studies, including text type, communicative mode, register, and discourse function. The taxonomy is therefore intended primarily as a practical hierarchical benchmarking framework for Arabic NLP research rather than a strict linguistic theory of genre.

AraGenre is intended to encourage research on hierarchical genre modelling, definition-guided classification, and robust Arabic genre understanding under realistic linguistic variation.

Welcome to the SlideGuard Artifact Detection Benchmark. This challenge evaluates your algorithm's ability to detect artifacts within tissue regions on Whole Slide Images (WSIs). The primary metric of the leaderboard is mean Dice score. You are allowed to post to leaderboard and remove from it as many submissions as you want - the intention is to allow you to post more than one method's results, however for the sake of benchmark clarity, we kindly ask you to be reasonable and only post the best result of each approach in case you tested many. 

To ensure fairness, all submissions are processed through a strictly standardized pipeline. Please read the instructions provided in "Preparing Submission" tab carefully, as failure to format your predictions correctly will result in an 'ERROR' on your scorecard, and a score of 0 for the missing, ill-formatted or wrongly named file.

title: CLEF 2026 JOKER Task 3: Onomastic Wordplay Translation from English to French
description:
The objective of the task is to translate onomastic (i.e., name-related) wordplay from English to French.
Such wordplay is widely used as a rhetorical device in novels, poetry, and plays. It is widespread in classic literature, such as in Shakespeare’s characters’ names, but also in names found in modern-day works such as Pokémon, Harry Potter, Asterix, and video games. Meaningful proper names in fictional universes are often neologisms. Neologisms – that is, newly coined words – are among the most common forms of linguistic creativity. Due to their highly idiosyncratic nature, neologisms – particularly humorous ones – are challenging for both humans and machines to translate.


Submission guidelines: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1u6xzlStni8XNrj1JpAYuFmK8KaT9I3psE5931QRCBuI/edit?usp=sharing](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1u6xzlStni8XNrj1JpAYuFmK8KaT9I3psE5931QRCBuI/edit?usp=sharing)

title: NLPCC 2026 Shared Task 6: The Second Shared Task on LLM-Generated Text Detection
description:
The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has given rise to a series of challenges, including the generation of disinformation, the spread of harmful content, and various forms of misuse. Against this backdrop, the efficient discrimination between LLM-generated text and human-written text has become an urgent and critical research issue in the field of natural language processing (NLP). While remarkable progress has been made, relevant research has largely focused on English, systematic and technical exploration for the Chinese remain scarce. This shared task aims to fill this gap, build more robust Chinese LLM-generated text detectors, and advance research and real-world applications in this field within the Chinese.

Following the success of the 1st Shared Task on LLM-Generated Text Detection (NLPCC 2025), the 2nd Shared Task on LLM-Generated Text Detection in 2026 features significant upgrades: the task formulation has been expanded from binary to ternary classification. Specifically, in addition to distinguishing between human-written text and LLM-generated text, a new category for identifying LLM-refined text has been introduced, which better aligns with real-world application scenarios of LLMs. Participating teams are required to design and implement text detection algorithms based on the training data provided to achieve accurate classification and will undergo rigorous stress testing.

title: NADI 2026  Task 2: Spoken Dialect Identification
description:
Part of the Nuanced Arabic Dialect Identification 2026 shared task, this Spoken Dialect Identification task focuses on out-of-domain dialect identification, where the final test set will be a blind set from an unknown domain. 

This year we focus on an out-of-domain Spoken dialect ID task. Language and dialect ID models may be somewhat prone to overfitting to a training domain, limiting their applicability in real world scenarios. This blind domain evaluation aims to test the generalizability of these models. For our baseline we provide a training script to finetune a pretrained ECAPA-TDNN language ID system  on a 200hr subset of the ADI-20 dataset. Training is unrestricted, and participants are free to train on the full ADI-17/20 datasets. Because this is a blind out-of-domain evaluation, we encourage participants to consider evaluating their models on selected data from other domains such as radio, read speech, conversational telephone etc.

title: RTPSeg Challenge
description:
Participants are required to develop a road-scene vehicle-borne LiDAR point cloud semantic segmentation algorithm based on multi-modal data from RTPSeg (LiDAR point clouds, RGB images, and thermal infrared images). The algorithm shall address the following key technical challenges:

(1) **Complex Illumination Conditions**: In degraded RGB scenarios such as nighttime and backlight, how to effectively fuse thermal radiation information from thermal infrared images to achieve accurate 3D semantic segmentation of road targets.

(2) **Multi-modal Heterogeneous Data Fusion**: How to handle cross-modal fusion challenges including sensor projection errors, inconsistent fields of view (FoV) among multiple sensors, mismatched spatial resolutions, and pixel‑level spatial misalignment.

(3) **Modality Gap Bridging and Complementary Exploitation**: How to overcome large modality gaps and fully leverage the texture/colour information from RGB images, thermal radiation information from thermal infrared images, and 3D geometric information from LiDAR point clouds.

**Semantic Categories**

The algorithm focuses on 18 semantic classes in urban and rural road scenes:
